A  In the early decades of the twentieth century, wolves were systematically killed throughout much of the western United States, including within Yellowstone, the country's first national park. By the mid-1920s, they had been eliminated there entirely. For seventy years the park had no wolves at all, until, in 1995 and 1996, several dozen were captured in Canada and released in Yellowstone in one of the most closely watched conservation projects ever undertaken. The population grew rapidly, and the wolves' return has since become one of the most celebrated stories in modern ecology.

B  The popular version of that story runs as follows. In the absence of wolves, elk had multiplied and grazed heavily on young willow and aspen trees, particularly along rivers. Once wolves returned, elk numbers fell and the survivors, fearing attack, avoided open valleys and riverbanks. Freed from constant browsing, trees and shrubs recovered; beavers, which depend on willow, returned; and the riverbanks, held together by roots, became more stable. This chain of effects, in which a predator at the top of a food web influences plants and even the physical landscape, is known as a trophic cascade. A short online video narrating this account has been viewed tens of millions of times.

C  There is genuine evidence for parts of this narrative. Elk numbers on the park's northern range did decline substantially after the wolves arrived, and in some places willow and aspen have grown taller than at any time in decades. The number of beaver colonies in the northern part of the park has also increased. Few ecologists doubt that wolves have contributed to these changes. The question is how much of the change they are responsible for, and here, I believe, the popular account claims considerably more than the evidence can support.

D  The difficulty is that wolves did not return to an otherwise unchanging environment. During the same period, the park's populations of grizzly bears and cougars, which also prey on elk, increased; human hunting of elk outside the park boundaries was heavy in some years; and a series of droughts reduced the food available to elk. Disentangling the effect of wolves from these other factors is extremely difficult. Moreover, the idea that fear of wolves alone keeps elk away from riverbanks has received mixed support: studies tracking elk with satellite collars have found that they do not avoid high-risk areas as consistently as the theory predicts.

E  Perhaps the most important lesson concerns the limits of recovery. Decades of heavy browsing allowed many streams to cut deeper into their beds, and with fewer beavers to build dams, the water table in some valleys fell. As a result, even where elk browsing has declined, willows in these areas have struggled to grow, because their roots can no longer reach water easily. Ecologists describe such a situation as an alternative stable state: once an ecosystem has changed sufficiently, simply restoring a missing species may not be enough to return it to its former condition.

F  None of this means that the reintroduction was a mistake; on the contrary, it restored a native predator to a landscape from which it had been wrongly removed, and it has taught scientists a great deal. But it does suggest that we should be wary of stories that are too neat. Ecosystems are complex, and the appealing image of a single species repairing an entire landscape risks creating unrealistic expectations for rewilding projects elsewhere. In my view, the real value of Yellowstone's wolves lies less in proving a simple theory than in revealing how much remains to be understood.

D  Recent research has begun to explain the durability of Roman concrete. In marine structures such as harbour walls, scientists reported in 2017 that seawater seeping through the concrete had reacted with the volcanic ash to form new minerals, including rare crystals that strengthened the material over time. Whereas modern concrete tends to deteriorate in seawater, Roman marine concrete appears to have become more cohesive. A further study published in 2023 examined small white lumps of lime found throughout Roman concrete, which had previously been dismissed as evidence of careless mixing. The researchers argued that these lumps resulted from mixing with quicklime at high temperatures and that they allowed cracks to heal themselves: when water entered a crack, it dissolved some of the lime, which then recrystallised and filled the gap.

E  Modern concrete, by contrast, is usually made with Portland cement, patented in England in 1824, and is typically reinforced with steel bars. This combination gives it far greater strength, particularly under tension, allowing the construction of tall buildings and long bridges that would have been impossible for the Romans. However, the steel is also a weakness. When water and salt penetrate the concrete, the steel corrodes and expands, causing the surrounding material to crack and eventually break away. Many structures built in the twentieth century now require costly repairs for this reason.

F  Could Roman techniques improve modern construction? Some researchers believe so, pointing out that producing cement accounts for around 8 per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions, and that materials incorporating volcanic ash or similar substances could reduce this impact while increasing durability. Yet Roman concrete is weaker than modern concrete and sets more slowly, making it unsuitable for many contemporary purposes. Rather than replacing modern methods, the ancient material is more likely to inspire new mixtures that combine the strengths of both.
